IIS worker (w3wp.exe) writing robots.txt / .php / .js into web root AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects IIS worker process writing or modifying SEO-fraud artifact files (robots.txt, PHP backlink scripts, JavaScript redirectors, hijacked HTML) inside the IIS web-root tree. Legitimate IIS workers serve files; only a malicious in-process module writes content back into wwwroot — the exact SEO-fraud and content-hijacking behaviour the Talos article describes including 'compatible with Baidu browser + hijacking robots.txt' and 'JavaScript redirectors, PHP backlink scripts'. Rationale: Article explicitly calls out 'compatible with Baidu browser + hijacking robots.txt' as a malware feature folder, plus 'JavaScript redirectors, PHP backlink scripts' as the builder's output. w3wp.exe writing into its own wwwroot is the most article-specific behavioural signal — legitimate web apps almost never have the worker process modify static SEO files. Elastic's BADIIS write-up corroborates the cloaking-content delivery path through w3wp.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/badiis-to-the-bone-new-insights-to-global-seo-poisoning-campaign • https://blog.alphahunt.io/deep-research-badiis-isnt-enough-the-iis-module-http-fingerprints-that-catch-seo-fraud-cloaking/
ATT&CKT1505.004 T1565.001 T1608.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress / CMS plugins running under w3wp.exe legitimately updating robots.txt or theme .php files
  • ASP.NET file-upload feature where the worker writes attachments into wwwroot (e.g. user-uploaded HTML/JS)
  • Yoast SEO / RankMath updating robots.txt programmatically through the web app
  • Custom application code writing log .html files into wwwroot for debugging
  • Web-deploy hot-swap of .js bundles by an in-process build pipeline
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !contains "-ap \"WordPress\"" | where FolderPath !has @"\App_Data\" and FolderPath !has @"\uploads\" and FolderPath !has @"\wp-content\uploads\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): inspect the written file content — does the .php contain href backlinks to gambling/adult/foreign-language sites? Does the .js perform location.replace() / window.location based on document.referrer or navigator.language? Does robots.txt allow paths that look promotional (e.g. /qp/, /casino/, foreign-language directories)? Step 2 (contain): if content is hijacked, isolate the IIS host, stop w3wp.exe, restore wwwroot from version-control / backup. Step 3 (hunt): grep wwwroot estate-wide for the same suspicious referer-keyed JS / PHP signatures; correlate to UC4 (applicationHost.config / module DLL drops) and UC2 (BadIIS C2 contacts) on the same host within ±24h to confirm the full BadIIS chain.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FileName =~ "robots.txt")
    or (FolderPath has @"\inetpub\wwwroot\" and (FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".js" or FileName endswith ".html" or FileName endswith ".htm"))
    or (FolderPath has @"\inetpub\" and FileName =~ "robots.txt")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName =~ "w3wp.exe" or ActingProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","Created","Modified")
| where (TargetFileName =~ "robots.txt")
    or (TargetFilePath has @"\inetpub\wwwroot\" and (TargetFileName endswith ".php" or TargetFileName endswith ".js" or TargetFileName endswith ".html" or TargetFileName endswith ".htm"))
    or (TargetFilePath has @"\inetpub\" and TargetFileName =~ "robots.txt")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: IIS Worker (w3wp.exe) Writing SEO-Fraud Artifacts to Web Root
id: 1f9e6a4c-2b7d-4e51-bc09-8d3f6c2a4e88
description: Detects w3wp.exe writing robots.txt or .php/.js/.html into the IIS wwwroot tree — the impact-phase footprint of the BadIIS demo.pdb commodity SEO-fraud variant (Talos May 2026), which performs Baidu browser cloaking, robots.txt hijacking, PHP backlink injection, and JS redirector deployment.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/from-pdb-strings-to-maas-tracking-a-commodity-badiis-ecosystem/
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/20
tags:
  - attack.t1505.004
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1608.006
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith: '\w3wp.exe'
  selection_target:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\inetpub\wwwroot\'
      - '\inetpub\'
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\robots.txt'
      - '.php'
      - '.js'
      - '.html'
      - '.htm'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_target
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\w3wp.exe OR *\\W3wp.exe OR *\\W3WP.EXE) (@TargetFilename:(*\\robots.txt OR *\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\*.php OR *\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\*.js OR *\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\*.html OR *\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\*.htm))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/\\w3wp\.exe$/i (TargetFileName=/\\robots\.txt$/i OR TargetFileName=/\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\.*\.(php|js|html|htm)$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name="w3wp.exe" AND (Filesystem.file_name="robots.txt" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\wwwroot\\*.php" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\wwwroot\\*.js" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\wwwroot\\*.html" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\inetpub\\*\\robots.txt") AND Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified","written") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name="w3wp.exe" AND (Filesystem.file_name="robots.txt" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\wwwroot\\*.php" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\wwwroot\\*.js" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\wwwroot\\*.html" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\inetpub\\*\\robots.txt") AND Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified","written") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write Installation High
Service install with binPath pointing to user-writeable path or LOLBin. Detects via process telemetry (sc.exe create) and registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\* writes).
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "create"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
// EventID 4697 is "Service installed" — direct signal, no cmdline-regex needed.
union
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4697
        | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName,
                  Detail = strcat("ServiceName=", ServiceName, " | Image=", ServiceFileName) ),
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where Account !endswith "$"
        | where NewProcessName endswith "\sc.exe" and CommandLine has "create"
        | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account,
                  Detail = strcat("4688 sc.exe create: ", CommandLine) )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Service Persistence via sc.exe with User-Writable Path
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0e
status: experimental
description: |
    sc.exe create with the binary path under \Users\, \AppData\,
    \ProgramData\, or \Temp\ — service-install persistence outside
    legitimate program directories.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1543.003
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_sc:
        Image|endswith: '\sc.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: 'create'
    selection_path:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '\Users\'
            - '\AppData\'
            - '\ProgramData\'
            - '\Temp\'
    condition: selection_sc and selection_path

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

      AND (Processes.process="*\Users\*" OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*"
        OR Processes.process="*\ProgramData\*" OR Processes.process="*\Temp\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\AppData\*"
            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\Temp\*")
        by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="sc.exe" AND Processes.process="*create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*\Users\*" OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*"
        OR Processes.process="*\ProgramData\*" OR Processes.process="*\Temp\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
        where Registry.registry_path="*\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\*"
          AND Registry.registry_value_name="ImagePath"
          AND (Registry.registry_value_data="*\Users\*"
            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\AppData\*"
            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\Temp\*")
        by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`]

Mini Shai-Hulud strikes again: npm worm compromises hundreds of @antv packages

AikidoStepSecurity
2026-05-19 14 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process-memory secret scraping via /proc · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Mini Shai-Hulud C2 exfil to t.m-kosche.com disguised as OpenTelemetry collector AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections/DNS to the campaign's fallback C2 t.m-kosche.com, which receives RSA-encrypted stolen credentials over OpenTelemetry-style paths (/api/public/otel/v1/traces) on 443. The domain is unique to this campaign and confirmed by multiple vendors, making any contact high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchored on the campaign-unique C2 domain t.m-kosche.com confirmed by StepSecurity, Microsoft, Snyk and JFrog write-ups; the OTel path /api/public/otel/v1/traces detail was added from cross-referenced sources. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/shai-hulud-here-we-go-again-mass-npm-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-antv-ecosystem • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/20/mini-shai-hulud-compromised-antv-npm-packages-enable-ci-cd-credential-theft/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-here-we-go-again-may19/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers/sandboxes deliberately detonating the sample and beaconing to the domain
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling resolving the IOC domain for reputation lookups
  • DNS sinkhole already redirecting m-kosche.com (resolution still logged)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/CI runner and the InitiatingProcess (node/npm/python) that resolved m-kosche.com; pull the surrounding process tree and any npm install in scope. 2) Contain: block t.m-kosche.com at egress/DNS, isolate the host, and freeze the associated CI pipeline; treat every secret reachable from that environment as compromised and begin rotation. 3) Hunt: pivot org-wide on the @antv/timeago/echarts-for-react package versions, search GitHub for repos created with the reversed 'niagA oG eW ereH' description, and check for .claude/.vscode persistence writes.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "m-kosche.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "m-kosche.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm payload by SHA256 AIInstallation Medium
Detects the worm's obfuscated payload file landing or executing on a host by its confirmed SHA256 hashes. High-fidelity exact-match IOC for the AntV-wave payload. Rationale: Uses the two pre-extracted SHA256 payload hashes as exact-match file/process IOCs — zero ambiguity, only ships because the campaign is documented by multiple vendors. Cross-checked against: • https://www.snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-here-we-go-again-may19/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst copying the sample onto an analysis VM
  • EDR quarantine/restore operations re-touching the file
  • Threat-intel YARA scanning repos that contain a stored copy of the sample
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path and the process that wrote/executed it; determine if this is a dev workstation or a CI runner. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the node/python chain, and rotate every credential reachable from the environment (AWS/GCP/Azure/K8s/Vault/npm tokens). 3) Hunt: sweep for the C2 domain m-kosche.com, the compromised @antv package versions in lockfiles, and .vscode/.claude persistence artifacts across the fleet.

GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process-memory secret scraping via /proc AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the worm's embedded Python helper that scans /proc for the Runner.Worker process and reads its memory to recover masked CI/CD secrets in plaintext. Targets Linux CI runners where a node/npm-spawned interpreter references Runner.Worker or /proc/<pid>/mem. Rationale: Anchored on the campaign-specific Runner.Worker /proc memory-scraping technique (the novel CI secret-recovery method) corroborated by Microsoft and the Securonix beta analytic; scoped to npm/node-spawned interpreters to cut noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/20/mini-shai-hulud-compromised-antv-npm-packages-enable-ci-cd-credential-theft/ • https://connect.securonix.com/threat-research-intelligence-62/beta-detection-mini-shai-hulud-runner-worker-memory-secret-extraction-analytic-308
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate CI debugging tooling (gdb, strace, custom memory profilers) inspecting Runner.Worker
  • Self-hosted runner health/diagnostic scripts that read /proc
  • Security agents legitimately scanning /proc memory
  • Performance profilers using process_vm_readv
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("gdb","strace","perf ","datadog-agent","falcon-sensor"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent is a node/npm install step rather than an approved diagnostic; capture the full command line and the package being installed. 2) Contain: cancel the workflow run, revoke the runner's token, and immediately rotate ALL repository/org Actions secrets (they must be assumed exfiltrated regardless of masking). 3) Hunt: check egress to m-kosche.com from the runner, review recent npm publishes from the same maintainer token, and audit GitHub for worm-created repos.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Runner.Worker" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/proc/self/mem","process_vm_readv") or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","npx","sh","bash","python","python3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "Runner.Worker" or SyslogMessage has_any ("/proc/self/mem","process_vm_readv")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("node","npm","python")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GitHub Actions Runner.Worker Memory Scrape (Mini Shai-Hulud)
id: 9c3f5e72-1d4a-4b8e-a0f6-2e7c8d4b1a90
description: Detects a process referencing Runner.Worker or reading /proc memory to extract CI/CD secrets, as used by the Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm
references:

detection:

      - '/proc/self/mem'
      - 'process_vm_readv'

source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:*Runner.Worker* OR @process.command_line:*/proc/self/mem* OR @process.command_line:*process_vm_readv*)

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*Runner.Worker*" OR Processes.process="*/proc/*/mem*" OR Processes.process="*process_vm_readv*") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node","npm","npx","sh","bash") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Mini Shai-Hulud persistence hooks written into .vscode/ and .claude/ configs AIInstallation Medium
Detects node/npm/npx processes writing into .vscode/ or .claude/ configuration directories, where the worm plants auto-execution hooks that survive across sessions and cloned repos. Combination of a JS toolchain process touching these trusted IDE/agent config dirs is the article-specific signal. Rationale: Anchored on the worm's documented persistence in .claude/ and .vscode/ trusted config dirs (Akamai/Microsoft); scopes to the JS toolchain (node/npm/npx) as the writing process to separate from normal IDE activity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/mini-shai-hulud-worm-returns-goes-public • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/20/mini-shai-hulud-compromised-antv-npm-packages-enable-ci-cd-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1554 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately running npm scripts that scaffold .vscode/settings.json or tasks.json
  • VS Code extension installers writing into .vscode
  • Project generators (create-react-app, nx, vite) emitting .vscode workspace configs
  • Claude Code itself writing into .claude during normal use
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("create-react-app","vite","nx ","yo ","degit") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written .vscode/tasks.json or .claude config and inspect for auto-run commands, embedded scripts, or network callouts; correlate with a recent npm install of an @antv/timeago package. 2) Contain: remove the malicious config entries, isolate the host, and rotate credentials accessible from the dev environment. 3) Hunt: check the host and any repos cloned from it for the same persistence files, look for egress to m-kosche.com, and search version control for committed .vscode/.claude hooks pushed by stolen tokens.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath contains ".vscode" or FolderPath contains ".claude"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.cmd","npm","npx.cmd","npx")
| where FileName endswith ".json" or FileName endswith ".js" or FileName endswith ".sh"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has ".vscode" or TargetFilePath has ".claude"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","npx")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142") or SHA1 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142") or MD5 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142") or SHA1 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142") or MD5 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

actions-cool/issues-helper GitHub Action Compromised: All Tags Point to Imposter Commit That Exfiltrates CI/CD Credentials

StepSecurity
2026-05-19 6 use cases 0 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The popular GitHub Action actions-cool/issues-helper has been compromised. Every existing tag in the repository has been moved to point to a single imposter commit that does not appear in the action's normal commit history. That commit contains malicious code that exfiltrates credentials from CI/CD pipelines that run the action.

Domainst.m-kosche.com

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] GitHub workflow references actions-cool/issues-helper or maintain-one-comment by tag
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — actions-cool/issues-helper GitHub Action Compromised: All Tags Point to Imposter
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] bun runtime executed on CI runner spawning python3 with sudo escalation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to t.m-kosche.com from CI/CD runner or any endpoint · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] python3 reading /proc/<PID>/mem to scrape Runner.Worker secrets
Outbound C2 to t.m-kosche.com from CI/CD runner or any endpoint AICommand & Control High
Hunts the exfiltration callback used by the compromised actions-cool/issues-helper and actions-cool/maintain-one-comment GitHub Actions. Any DNS resolution or HTTPS connection to t.m-kosche.com from a runner, developer workstation, or build agent indicates secrets-in-flight exfiltration. Rationale: Pure-IOC detection on t.m-kosche.com — the attacker-controlled exfil domain named explicitly in the StepSecurity advisory and corroborated by The Hacker News, GBHackers, and SC Media. The domain is on the Harden-Runner global block list. Cross-checked with the StepSecurity X post and the Mini Shai-Hulud cluster note from coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/actions-cool-issues-helper-github-action-compromised-all-tags-point-to-imposter-commit-that-exfiltrates-ci-cd-credentials • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/github-actions-supply-chain-attack.html • https://gbhackers.com/compromised-github-action/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/compromised-github-action-exfiltrates-workflow-credentials/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate research traffic from a sandbox / detonation chamber that intentionally resolves IOC domains
  • Threat-intel platforms (MISP, ThreatConnect) doing enrichment lookups against the domain
  • Security analyst manually browsing the StepSecurity advisory and clicking embedded IOC links
  • Harden-Runner audit-mode telemetry that intentionally allows the call so it can be logged before blocking
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonation","misp","threatintel") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the source host/runner from DeviceName / ClientIP / aid. Pull the full process tree on the source (parent process of the resolver / connector — look for bun, node, python3). 2. Contain: if a self-hosted runner, pull the runner offline; if a developer workstation, isolate the endpoint. Rotate ANY secrets exposed to recent workflow runs on the affected repository, especially GITHUB_TOKEN, repo secrets, and OIDC-issued cloud credentials. 3. Hunt: enumerate every workflow run in the org that referenced actions-cool/issues-helper or actions-cool/maintain-one-comment in the last 30 days; pin all third-party actions to immutable commit SHAs going forward; search audit logs for unauthorized PRs/commits made with the leaked GITHUB_TOKEN.

(DeviceNetworkEvents

  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType),
(DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType in ("DnsQueryResponse","ConnectionSuccess")
  | where RemoteUrl has exfil_domain or AdditionalFields has exfil_domain
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, AdditionalFields)
| order by Timestamp desc
let exfil_domain = "m-kosche.com";
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has exfil_domain | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ServerIPAddress),
(CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationHostName has exfil_domain or RequestURL has exfil_domain or DestinationDnsDomain has exfil_domain | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, SourceUserName),
(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has exfil_domain | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsQueryType, DnsResponseName),
(ImWebSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Url has exfil_domain or HttpHostName has exfil_domain | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

python3 reading /proc/<PID>/mem to scrape Runner.Worker secrets AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact credential-harvesting primitive used by the compromised actions-cool actions: a python3 process opening another process's /proc/<PID>/mem to scrape decrypted GitHub Actions secrets from Runner.Worker memory. The behaviour is rare on legitimate CI/CD runners and developer Linux endpoints. Rationale: Anchors on the exact behaviour the article and StepSecurity Harden-Runner traces describe: python3 reading /proc/<PID>/mem against the Runner.Worker process (PID 2119 in their controlled test) and grep-filtering for `isSecret`:true tokens. Cross-process /proc/<PID>/mem reads by python on Linux are a high-fidelity credential-access signal — this is essentially T1003.007 in script form. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/actions-cool-issues-helper-github-action-compromised-all-tags-point-to-imposter-commit-that-exfiltrates-ci-cd-credentials • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/github-actions-supply-chain-attack.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/007/
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552.001 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR teams running memory acquisition tools (avml, lime, volatility) on Linux endpoints
  • Developers debugging their own application by reading /proc/self/mem
  • Container security scanners that introspect process memory of running workloads
  • Performance-profiling agents (py-spy, pyflame) that attach to other Python processes
  • Legitimate use of bun/node memory analysis tooling during CI for performance regression tests
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("avml","lime","volatility","py-spy","strace","gdb") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("avml","lime","strace","gdb")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the python3 invocation's parent process tree. If parent is `bun` or the GitHub Actions runner (`Runner.Listener` / `Runner.Worker`), it's the attack chain — almost no legitimate workflow shells from bun into python3 reading runner memory. Pull the full command line and resolve the PID being read. 2. Contain: kill the python3 process, take the runner offline, snapshot disk for IR. Rotate every secret that ever touched that runner's workflows in the last 30d (GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC-issued cloud creds, registry credentials, repo / org / environment secrets). 3. Hunt: search org-wide for the same parent→child chain (bun → python3 → /proc/*/mem) and for any callbacks to t.m-kosche.com or related Mini Shai-Hulud infrastructure; audit recent commits and PRs created via affected GITHUB_TOKENs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName matches regex @"^python3?(\.\d+)?$" or InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"^python3?(\.\d+)?$"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/\d+/mem"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("isSecret","Runner.Worker")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/\d+/mem"
| extend ProcMemTarget = extract(@"/proc/(\d+)/mem", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, ProcMemTarget, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 30d;
union isfuzzy=true
(Syslog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
  | where Facility in ("authpriv","auth","daemon","user")
  | where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)python3?[^\s]*\s+[^\n]*/proc/\d+/mem"
     or SyslogMessage has_any ("isSecret","Runner.Worker")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage),
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
  | where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)python3?(\.\d+)?$"
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/\d+/mem"
     or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("isSecret","Runner.Worker")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Python Process Reading /proc/<PID>/mem (CI Runner Memory Scrape)
id: 2b8f1a64-3d97-4d8c-9c0e-1b2af3b6e711
status: experimental
description: Detects a python interpreter executed with a /proc/<PID>/mem path in its command line, the credential-dump primitive used by the compromised actions-cool/issues-helper and actions-cool/maintain-one-comment GitHub Actions to scrape Runner.Worker memory and exfiltrate decrypted secrets tagged "isSecret":true.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/actions-cool-issues-helper-github-action-compromised-all-tags-point-to-imposter-commit-that-exfiltrates-ci-cd-credentials
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/github-actions-supply-chain-attack.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/20
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1003.007
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|re: '/proc/\d+/mem'
  selection_str:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'isSecret'
      - 'Runner.Worker'
  condition: selection_proc and (selection_cmd or selection_str)
falsepositives:
  - Forensic / memory-acquisition tooling (volatility, lime, avml) operated by IR teams
  - Debugging by developers reading their own process memory for diagnostics
level: high
source:(linux.auditd OR linux.syslog) (@process.executable.path:(*/python3 OR */python OR */python3.* OR */PYTHON3) OR @process.name:(python3 OR python OR PYTHON3)) (@process.command_line:*\/proc\/* AND @process.command_line:*\/mem*) OR @process.command_line:*isSecret* OR @process.command_line:*Runner.Worker*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/python3?(\.\d+)?$/i | regex("/proc/\d+/mem|isSecret|Runner\.Worker", field=CommandLine) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count()) | sort(field=_count, order=desc)
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("python","python3") AND (Processes.process="*/proc/*/mem*" OR Processes.process="*isSecret*" OR Processes.process="*Runner.Worker*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(cmdline, "(?i)/proc/\d+/mem") OR match(cmdline, "(?i)isSecret|Runner\.Worker")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("python","python3") AND (Processes.process="*/proc/*/mem*" OR Processes.process="*isSecret*" OR Processes.process="*Runner.Worker*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(cmdline, "(?i)/proc/\d+/mem") OR match(cmdline, "(?i)isSecret|Runner\.Worker")
bun runtime executed on CI runner spawning python3 with sudo escalation AIInstallation High
Hunts the install-stage of the actions-cool/issues-helper compromise: the imposter commit's index.js downloads the bun JavaScript runtime onto the runner, which then spawns python3 via sudo to read Runner.Worker memory. The bun→python3→sudo chain is the article's signature behaviour. Rationale: Anchors on the article's verbatim chain: `bun` runtime (which the imposter commit explicitly downloads to the runner) spawning python3, sudo, and `gh auth token`. This combination is essentially unique to the attack — bun is a JS runtime, not a Python wrapper, and bun→sudo is anomalous in any normal CI workflow. Cross-checked against StepSecurity Harden-Runner test run capture (linked in advisory) and confirmed by Hacker News + GBHackers coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/actions-cool-issues-helper-github-action-compromised-all-tags-point-to-imposter-commit-that-exfiltrates-ci-cd-credentials • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/github-actions-supply-chain-attack.html • https://gbhackers.com/compromised-github-action/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1548.003 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A bun-based project's postinstall script that legitimately shells out to a Python build helper (rare in practice)
  • Developer workstations where bun is used as a general-purpose script runner and the user manually invokes sudo / gh from a bun REPL
  • CI workflows that intentionally use bun to orchestrate multi-language builds with Python steps
  • Bun's own self-update mechanism invoking sudo to install to /usr/local
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "bun" and FileName == "sudo" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("apt-get","dnf","yum","npm install -g","bun upgrade"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the GitHub Actions workflow run identifier from the runner's environment and confirm whether the workflow referenced actions-cool/issues-helper or actions-cool/maintain-one-comment (by tag — anything other than a pinned full commit SHA is suspect). Capture the bun binary's hash and origin (was it downloaded from bun.sh during the run? from an attacker-controlled URL?). 2. Contain: stop the runner, revoke its registration token, rotate GITHUB_TOKEN and every workflow-accessible secret. If self-hosted, image-rebuild the runner from scratch. 3. Hunt: org-wide search for any workflow file (YAML in .github/workflows/) that uses these two actions by tag rather than by SHA; enforce a Compromised Actions Policy and pinning policy; review last 30d of commits/PRs/releases by the GITHUB_TOKEN actor on affected repos.
let lookback = 30d;
let BunHosts = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
    | where FileName =~ "bun" or FolderPath endswith "/bun" or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(curl|wget)[^\n]*bun\.sh"
    | project BunTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, BunPid = ProcessId, BunCmd = ProcessCommandLine, BunParent = InitiatingProcessFileName;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "bun"
| where FileName in~ ("python","python3","sudo","gh")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gh auth token","sudo python3","/proc/","isSecret")
| join kind=inner BunHosts on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (BunTime .. BunTime + 10m)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, BunTime, BunCmd, BunParent, ChildImage = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, ChildSha256 = SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 30d;
let BunHosts = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where ActingProcessName endswith "/bun" or ActingProcessName =~ "bun" or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(curl|wget)[^\n]*bun\.sh"
    | project BunTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, BunPid = ActingProcessId, BunCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where ParentProcessName endswith "/bun" or ParentProcessName =~ "bun"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)/(python3?|sudo|gh)$"
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("gh auth token","sudo python3","/proc/","isSecret")
| join kind=inner BunHosts on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (BunTime .. BunTime + 10m)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, BunCmd, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: bun Runtime Spawning python3/sudo/gh-auth-token on Linux (actions-cool Compromise)
id: c8a4b2e1-7d61-4c30-9f12-5e3a1c9b4a07
status: experimental
description: Detects the bun JavaScript runtime executing python3, sudo, or `gh auth token` as a child process — the exact in-runner chain used by the compromised actions-cool/issues-helper and actions-cool/maintain-one-comment GitHub Actions to harvest Runner.Worker secrets.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/actions-cool-issues-helper-github-action-compromised-all-tags-point-to-imposter-commit-that-exfiltrates-ci-cd-credentials
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/github-actions-supply-chain-attack.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering

tags:

  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.t1548.003
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  parent_bun:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/bun'
  child_signal:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/sudo'
      - '/gh'

level: high
source:(linux.auditd OR linux.syslog) (@process.parent.executable.path:(*/bun OR */BUN) OR @process.parent.name:(bun OR BUN)) AND (@process.name:(python3 OR python OR sudo OR gh) OR @process.command_line:(*"gh auth token"* OR *"sudo python3"* OR *"/proc/"* OR *isSecret*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^bun$/i | regex("/python3?$|/sudo$|/gh$", field=ImageFileName) OR regex("gh auth token|sudo python3|/proc/\d+/mem|isSecret", field=CommandLine) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count()) | sort(field=_count, order=desc)

GitHub workflow references actions-cool/issues-helper or maintain-one-comment by tag AIDelivery High
Hunts use of the compromised GitHub Actions in any repository referenced by tag (or by a moved-tag SHA) rather than a pinned, audited full commit SHA. Anything other than a pinned SHA on the pre-compromise commit history will pull the imposter commit on next run. Rationale: Pure-IOC supply-chain detection on the two actions named by StepSecurity and corroborated by The Hacker News (`actions-cool/issues-helper` and `actions-cool/maintain-one-comment` — same actor, identical TTP). GitHub disabled the upstream repos, but any pre-existing pinned reference by tag or by a moved-tag SHA in a workflow YAML still resolves to the imposter commit on the next run until the workflow is patched. Detection should fire at workflow-prepare time (GitHub audit logs) and again on any commit/PR that adds such a reference. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/actions-cool-issues-helper-github-action-compromised-all-tags-point-to-imposter-commit-that-exfiltrates-ci-cd-credentials • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/github-actions-supply-chain-attack.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/compromised-github-action-exfiltrates-workflow-credentials/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1199
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-team test repository deliberately referencing the compromised action to validate the StepSecurity Compromised Actions Policy is working
  • Threat-research fork that retains the upstream reference for analysis purposes (should be sandboxed and offline)
  • Pinned full-commit-SHA references that map to KNOWN-GOOD pre-compromise commits (must verify the SHA pre-dates 2026-05-18 17:00 UTC and is reachable from the legitimate default branch — not the imposter dangling commit)
Response runbook
1. Triage: enumerate every repository in the org that references either action; pull the exact ref (tag, branch, or full commit SHA) used. For SHA references, verify the SHA is reachable from the repository's legitimate default-branch history (the imposter commit 1c9e803 is dangling and unreachable). 2. Contain: open emergency PRs to remove or replace the action across all affected workflows; enforce a repository ruleset that requires immutable SHA pinning on third-party actions; enable Harden-Runner or StepSecurity Compromised Actions Policy org-wide. 3. Hunt: rotate GITHUB_TOKENs and downstream secrets for any repo whose workflows ran the action since 2026-05-18 17:00 UTC; correlate against UC1 (t.m-kosche.com callbacks) to see which runners actually exfiltrated; review audit logs for unauthorized git pushes, tag manipulation, or PR creation events made by GITHUB_TOKEN actors during the affected window.
let lookback = 30d;
let compromised_actions = dynamic(["actions-cool/issues-helper","actions-cool/maintain-one-comment"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(GitHubAuditLog_CL

  | where Action_s has_any ("workflows.completed_workflow_run","workflows.created_workflow_run","workflows.prepared_workflow_job")
  | where RawData_s has_any (compromised_actions) or AdditionalFields_s has_any (compromised_actions)
  | project TimeGenerated, Actor_s, Repository_s, Action_s, RawData_s),
(GitHubRepoLogs
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
  | where AdditionalFields has_any (compromised_actions)
  | project TimeGenerated, Actor=tostring(AdditionalFields.actor), Repo=tostring(AdditionalFields.repository), Workflow=tostring(AdditionalFields.workflow), Reference=tostring(AdditionalFields.action_ref))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Active Supply Chain Attack: Malicious node-ipc Versions Published to npm

StepSecurity
2026-05-19 13 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Active Supply Chain Attack: Malicious node-ipc Versions Published to npm StepSecurity has detected multiple malicious releases of the popular node-ipc npm package. Three versions are currently known to be compromised, containing an obfuscated payload designed to steal cloud credentials, SSH keys, and CI/CD secrets. Our team is actively analyzing the attack, and this post will be updated as our investigation progresses

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Active Supply Chain Attack: Malicious node-ipc Versions Published to npm
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Compromised node-ipc.cjs bundle write (~117KB) under node_modules · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] node-ipc C2 callback to sh.azurestaticprovider.net (May 2026 npm supply-chain) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Node.js process bulk-reading cloud & SCM credential files in single session · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
node-ipc C2 callback to sh.azurestaticprovider.net (May 2026 npm supply-chain) AICommand & Control High
Detects any DNS lookup or outbound network connection to sh.azurestaticprovider.net, the credential-exfiltration C2 used by the malicious node-ipc versions 9.1.6 / 9.2.3 / 12.0.1 published 2026-05-14. The domain is a typosquat of azurestaticapps.net and has no legitimate business use — first sighting is incident-level signal. Rationale: Anchored on the literal C2 domain sh.azurestaticprovider.net pulled from the article's deobfuscated payload config (the 'r' field of the _0x501a65 attack config object). Domain typosquats Azure infrastructure and has no benign use — single-hit alerting tier is appropriate. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.npmjs.com/package/node-ipc
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / DFIR team intentionally resolving the domain during analysis from a sandboxed environment
  • Threat-intel feed validation tools that pre-resolve known-bad indicators (e.g. MISP, OpenCTI enrichment pipelines)
  • Internal IOC-detonation lab that mirrors npm packages to test detections
  • Network proxy doing pre-fetch / category lookup against the domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "VirusTotal"   // exclude analyst lookups; keep all other traffic
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the initiating process and parent — if it's node.exe / node, immediately check `npm ls node-ipc` / `package-lock.json` on the host for versions 9.1.6, 9.2.3, or 12.0.1. Pull the node-ipc.cjs file and confirm size > 80KB. Step 2 (contain): isolate the host from network, kill the offending node process, and block sh.azurestaticprovider.net at the proxy/firewall. Treat every cloud credential present on the host (AWS, Azure, GCP, GitHub PAT, SSH key, Kube token, Terraform state, npm token) as compromised — rotate immediately. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on DeviceNetworkEvents for the same domain across the fleet for the last 30 days; pivot on DeviceFileEvents for any node_modules/node-ipc/node-ipc.cjs writes since 2026-05-14; audit CI/CD job logs for npm install events of node-ipc.
// node-ipc supply-chain C2: any host contacting sh.azurestaticprovider.net
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "azurestaticprovider.net" or RemoteUrl =~ "sh.azurestaticprovider.net"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"     // exclude machine-account noise
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
// node-ipc supply-chain C2 — union across DNS + CEF/firewall + ASIM tables
let SuspectDomain = "azurestaticprovider.net";
let StartTime = ago(30d);
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
     | where TimeGenerated > StartTime
     | where Name has SuspectDomain
     | project TimeGenerated, Source = "DnsEvents", Host = Computer, ClientIP, QueriedName = Name, QueryType),
  (CommonSecurityLog
     | where TimeGenerated > StartTime
     | where DestinationHostName has SuspectDomain or RequestURL has SuspectDomain
     | project TimeGenerated, Source = "CommonSecurityLog", Host = SourceHostName, SrcIP = SourceIP, DstHost = DestinationHostName, DstIP = DestinationIP, URL = RequestURL),
  (ImNetworkSession
     | where TimeGenerated > StartTime
     | where DstHostname has SuspectDomain or DstDomain has SuspectDomain or Url has SuspectDomain
     | project TimeGenerated, Source = "ImNetworkSession", Host = SrcHostname, SrcIP = SrcIpAddr, DstHost = DstHostname, DstIP = DstIpAddr, URL = Url),
  (ImDnsActivity
     | where TimeGenerated > StartTime
     | where DnsQuery has SuspectDomain or DnsQueryName has SuspectDomain
     | project TimeGenerated, Source = "ImDnsActivity", Host = SrcHostname, SrcIP = SrcIpAddr, QueriedName = DnsQuery)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised node-ipc.cjs bundle write (~117KB) under node_modules AIInstallation High
Detects file-write events targeting `node_modules/node-ipc/node-ipc.cjs` whose payload exceeds 80KB after 2026-05-14, indicating installation of the malicious versions 9.1.6 / 9.2.3 / 12.0.1. The clean 12.0.0 bundle was ~37KB / 1269 lines; the trojanised bundle is ~117KB / 1271 lines with an 80KB obfuscated IIFE appended after the final module.exports. Rationale: Anchored on the exact file path (`node_modules/node-ipc/node-ipc.cjs`) and size delta (37KB clean → 117KB compromised, +80KB IIFE) called out in the article's diff block. The publication-date floor (2026-05-14) eliminates legitimate historical writes; the file-size predicate eliminates any future legitimate node-ipc release that doesn't add a comparable bundle. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.npmjs.com/package/node-ipc?activeTab=versions
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped lab environments restoring a snapshot of node-ipc 12.0.0 where prior tarball already exceeded 80KB due to legitimate fork patches
  • CI cache restoration from a vendored node_modules tarball captured pre-compromise (rare in 2026 — most teams don't vendor node_modules anymore)
  • Custom internal node-ipc fork that legitimately ships extra debug instrumentation in the .cjs bundle
  • Defender / Sysmon picking up the file write twice (rename then create) when npm rewrites the tarball — dedup on (DeviceId, FolderPath, FileSize)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("backup.exe","veeam.backup.shell.exe","snapraid.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "restore")   // exclude backup-restore noise
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): compute SHA256 of the written node-ipc.cjs and compare against the legitimate 12.0.0 hash; check the parent process — should be npm/yarn/pnpm. Confirm by `npm view node-ipc@<installed-version> dist.tarball` and inspecting the install metadata. Step 2 (contain): kill any running node process on the host, delete node_modules and package-lock.json, pin to node-ipc@11.1.0 or @12.0.0 in package.json with a npm-shrinkwrap.json lock, run `npm install --ignore-scripts` from a clean cache (`npm cache clean --force`). Treat all cloud / SCM / DB credentials accessible from this host or its CI runner as compromised — rotate. Step 3 (hunt): query DeviceFileEvents fleet-wide for the same FolderPath pattern since 2026-05-14; correlate with DNS lookups to sh.azurestaticprovider.net (UC1); audit npm audit logs / Artifactory / Verdaccio / proxy registries for the bad version tags being requested.
// Malicious node-ipc bundle write — anomalous .cjs size under node_modules
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > datetime(2026-05-14T00:00:00Z)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has @"\node_modules\node-ipc\" or FolderPath has "/node_modules/node-ipc/"
| where FileName =~ "node-ipc.cjs"
| where FileSize > 80000     // clean ~37KB; trojanised ~117KB (80KB IIFE injected)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Malicious node-ipc bundle write (ASIM file event)
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > datetime(2026-05-14T00:00:00Z)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\node_modules\node-ipc\" or TargetFilePath has "/node_modules/node-ipc/"
| where TargetFileName =~ "node-ipc.cjs"
| where TargetFileSize > 80000   // clean ~37KB; trojanised ~117KB
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:

Node.js process bulk-reading cloud & SCM credential files in single session AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for a single node process that opens >=3 distinct categories of credential artifacts (AWS, SSH, Kubernetes, Azure, GCP, GitHub CLI, Terraform, Docker, npm, Claude / Kiro IDE, shell history) within a single process lifetime. The compromised node-ipc payload harvests over 90 categories of secrets on require() — a fan-out pattern that no legitimate node tool produces in a single session. Rationale: The article enumerates 90+ credential categories the payload sweeps — AWS, Azure, GCP, SSH, Kubernetes, GitHub CLI, Claude AI, Kiro IDE, Terraform state, shell history. Mass fan-out from a single node PID is a behaviour pattern no legitimate dev tool exhibits in a single session. Sigma omitted because the detection requires aggregation across multiple file-open events keyed by process ID. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555 T1083 T1530
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Pulumi / AWS CDK / Terraform CDK runs — these node-based IaC tools legitimately read ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.kube/config, and ~/.terraform.d/ in a single invocation
  • Backstage / Cortex / similar developer-portal CLIs that aggregate credentials for multi-cloud dashboards
  • Local dev-experience scripts (e.g. `dev login` wrappers) that source AWS + Azure + GCP creds at once for a multi-cloud session
  • VSCode + extensions launched via node.exe reading .gitconfig + .npmrc + .claude/ as part of normal IDE startup
  • Security tools themselves — Snyk / Trivy / Semgrep CLIs sometimes inspect credential files for misconfig scanning
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("cdk","pulumi","terraform","snyk","trivy","semgrep","backstage","@cdktf","aws-sdk") and DistinctCredPaths < 6)   // suppress known multi-cloud IaC tooling unless fan-out is very wide
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the node process — pull its full command line and working directory; check whether node-ipc is in the resolved module graph (`lsof -p <pid> | grep node-ipc` on Linux, ProcessExplorer on Windows). Cross-check the host against UC1 (sh.azurestaticprovider.net contact) and UC2 (compromised .cjs file on disk). Step 2 (contain): if any of UC1/UC2 corroborate, kill the node process, isolate the host, and rotate every credential whose file was opened (start with cloud root/IAM keys, GitHub PATs, SSH keys, kube admin tokens). Step 3 (hunt): list every host the same user identity has touched in the last 30 days (lateral exposure); search for outbound HTTPS to any new azure-themed subdomain since 2026-05-14; audit private repos and cloud resources for the rotated credentials' last-used activity to identify what the attacker already accessed.
// node process touching multiple credential-store paths in one session — post-require('node-ipc') harvest pattern
let CredPathSubstrings = dynamic([
    @"\.aws\credentials", @"\.aws\config",
    @"\.ssh\id_rsa", @"\.ssh\id_ed25519", @"\.ssh\id_ecdsa", @"\.ssh\known_hosts",
    @"\.kube\config",
    @"\.azure\accessTokens", @"\.azure\azureProfile",
    @"\.config\gcloud\", @"\.config\gh\",
    @"\.terraform.d\", @"\.docker\config.json",
    @"\.npmrc", @"\.netrc", @"\.gitconfig",
    @"\.claude\", @"\.kiro\",
    @"\.bash_history", @"\.zsh_history", @"\.psql_history",
    "/.aws/", "/.ssh/", "/.kube/", "/.azure/",
    "/.config/gcloud/", "/.config/gh/", "/.terraform.d/",
    "/.docker/config.json", "/.npmrc", "/.netrc", "/.gitconfig",
    "/.claude/", "/.kiro/", "/.bash_history", "/.zsh_history"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| extend FullPath = strcat(FolderPath, FileName)
| where FullPath has_any (CredPathSubstrings)
| summarize DistinctCredPaths = dcount(FullPath),
            CredFilesSample = make_set(FullPath, 30),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleCmdLine = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCreationTime, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where DistinctCredPaths >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
// node process touching multiple credential-store paths in one session (ASIM file event)
let CredPathSubstrings = dynamic([
    @"\.aws\credentials", @"\.aws\config",
    @"\.ssh\id_rsa", @"\.ssh\id_ed25519", @"\.ssh\id_ecdsa",
    @"\.kube\config", @"\.azure\accessTokens", @"\.azure\azureProfile",
    @"\.config\gcloud\", @"\.config\gh\", @"\.terraform.d\",
    @"\.docker\config.json", @"\.npmrc", @"\.netrc", @"\.gitconfig",
    @"\.claude\", @"\.kiro\", @"\.bash_history", @"\.zsh_history",
    "/.aws/", "/.ssh/", "/.kube/", "/.azure/",
    "/.config/gcloud/", "/.config/gh/", "/.terraform.d/",
    "/.docker/config.json", "/.npmrc", "/.netrc", "/.gitconfig",
    "/.claude/", "/.kiro/", "/.bash_history", "/.zsh_history"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","/node","\\node")
| extend FullPath = TargetFilePath
| where FullPath has_any (CredPathSubstrings)
| summarize DistinctCredPaths = dcount(FullPath),
            CredFilesSample = make_set(FullPath, 30),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleCmdLine = any(ActingProcessCommandLine)
            by DvcHostname, ActingProcessId, ActorUsername
| where DistinctCredPaths >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
(@process.name:(node OR node.exe) OR @process.executable.name:(node OR node.exe)) AND (@file.path:(*/.aws/credentials* OR */.aws/config* OR */.ssh/id_rsa* OR */.ssh/id_ed25519* OR */.ssh/id_ecdsa* OR */.kube/config* OR */.azure/accessTokens* OR */.azure/azureProfile* OR */.config/gcloud/* OR */.config/gh/* OR */.terraform.d/* OR */.docker/config.json OR */.npmrc OR */.netrc OR */.gitconfig OR */.claude/* OR */.kiro/* OR */.bash_history OR */.zsh_history) OR @auditd.SYSCALL.path:(*/.aws/credentials* OR */.ssh/id_rsa* OR */.kube/config* OR */.azure/* OR */.config/gcloud/* OR */.terraform.d/* OR */.docker/config.json OR */.npmrc OR */.netrc OR */.gitconfig OR */.claude/* OR */.kiro/*))
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/[\\\/]node(\.exe)?$/i
| TargetFileName=/(\.aws[\\\/](credentials|config)|\.ssh[\\\/]id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|\.kube[\\\/]config|\.azure[\\\/](accessTokens|azureProfile)|\.config[\\\/](gcloud|gh)[\\\/]|\.terraform\.d[\\\/]|\.docker[\\\/]config\.json|\.npmrc|\.netrc|\.gitconfig|\.claude[\\\/]|\.kiro[\\\/]|\.bash_history|\.zsh_history)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId, UserName], function={ DistinctCredFiles := count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true) | sampleFiles := collect([TargetFileName], limit=30) | first := min(@timestamp) | last := max(@timestamp) })
| DistinctCredFiles >= 3

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium
Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)

| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)
| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20
| order by qcount desc
// ASIM ImDnsActivity normalises Windows DNS, Sysmon EID 22, Linux dnsmasq, etc.
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)

| summarize Queries = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(DnsQuery)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
