Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("bf9d8c0c3ed3ceaa831a13de27f1b1c7c7b7f01d2db4103bfdba4191940b0301") or SHA1 in~ ("bf9d8c0c3ed3ceaa831a13de27f1b1c7c7b7f01d2db4103bfdba4191940b0301") or MD5 in~ ("bf9d8c0c3ed3ceaa831a13de27f1b1c7c7b7f01d2db4103bfdba4191940b0301")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("bf9d8c0c3ed3ceaa831a13de27f1b1c7c7b7f01d2db4103bfdba4191940b0301") or SHA1 in~ ("bf9d8c0c3ed3ceaa831a13de27f1b1c7c7b7f01d2db4103bfdba4191940b0301") or MD5 in~ ("bf9d8c0c3ed3ceaa831a13de27f1b1c7c7b7f01d2db4103bfdba4191940b0301")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["bf9d8c0c3ed3ceaa831a13de27f1b1c7c7b7f01d2db4103bfdba4191940b0301"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mini Shai-Hulud Hits AntV: 300+ Malicious npm Packages Published via Compromised Maintainer Account

Snyk
2026-05-18 14 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A compromised npm maintainer account triggered an automated burst of over 300 malicious package versions across 323 packages in the AntV data visualization ecosystem, part of the ongoing Mini Shai-Hulud supply chain worm campaign. Here's what the malware does, how to detect exposure, and how to respond.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Mini Shai-Hulud Hits AntV: 300+ Malicious npm Packages Published via Compromised
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud npm preinstall hook spawning bun runtime · [LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud Claude Code SessionStart hook injection via npm install · [LLM] VS Code tasks.json folderOpen persistence written by npm install chain · [LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud Linux daemon persistence: kitty/cat.py and systemd user service · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud C2 backchannel: python polling GitHub commit search for 'firedalazer' · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud GitHub dead-drop exfiltration via python-requests/2.31.0
Mini Shai-Hulud npm preinstall hook spawning bun runtime AIInstallation High
Detects npm/node spawning the bun JavaScript runtime to execute a root-level index.js — the exact lifecycle pattern the May 2026 AntV supply-chain attack uses to fire 498KB obfuscated payload during npm install of @antv/g6, echarts-for-react, size-sensor, timeago.js and 319 other packages. bun is rarely a legitimate npm child in enterprise CI/dev environments. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim 'preinstall': 'bun run index.js' lifecycle hook combined with the article's named parent context (npm install). Bun-as-child-of-npm has near-zero legitimate baseline in dev/CI fleets outside the Bun ecosystem itself. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Bun-native projects where bun is genuinely listed as a runtime dependency (rare; usually invoked as bunx not via index.js)
  • Developer testing a local index.js script via bun in a node_modules-bootstrap shell where npm-init ran moments earlier
  • Internal supply-chain self-hosting where a vetted private package legitimately uses bun as a build tool
  • CI image building tests using bun runner to validate node packages
  • Monorepo tooling like Turborepo orchestrating mixed runtimes
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--ignore-scripts","bunx ") and ProcessCommandLine !has "preinstall") | where not (FolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Bun\\" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName == "explorer.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — pull the SHA256 of the bun binary and the parent npm command. Identify the package and version being installed (look at InitiatingProcessParentCommandLine or recent npm-cli.log on host). Cross-reference the package against the 323 AntV-wave compromised package list. Step 2: Contain — isolate host via Defender Live Response or CrowdStrike RTR. Kill the bun process tree. Block outbound to t.m-kosche.com at egress proxy. If on a developer workstation with cloud credentials present, immediately rotate all AWS/GCP/Azure/GitHub/npm tokens that were on disk. Step 3: Hunt — query DeviceFileEvents for .claude/, .vscode/, ~/.local/share/kitty/ writes by the same InitiatingProcessId. Pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for api.github.com and t.m-kosche.com beacons from this host. Check for new repos under the user's GitHub account with Dune-themed names.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm","npm.exe","node","node.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","yarn install","pnpm install")
| where FileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "index.js"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","/npm","/node")
    or CommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","yarn install","pnpm install")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\bun.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/bun"
| where CommandLine has "index.js"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mini Shai-Hulud Claude Code SessionStart hook injection via npm install AIInstallation High
Detects npm/node/bun writing .claude/settings.json or .claude/setup.mjs, the AI-coding-agent hijack used by the AntV wave to re-execute the credential-harvesting payload every time a developer opens a new Claude Code session in an infected workspace. Legitimate Claude Code settings are authored by the user via the IDE, never by an install lifecycle process. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim persistence path '.claude/settings.json with a SessionStart hook executing node .claude/setup.mjs'. Pairing the file path with an npm-family writer is high-fidelity because Claude Code settings are normally authored by Code.exe / claude CLI itself, never by node during an install. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate npm-installed dev tool that genuinely modifies .claude config (e.g. claude-mem MCP plugin auto-config — rare and should be allowlisted explicitly)
  • Postinstall script of an enterprise-vetted CLI that writes .claude/settings.json for organization defaults
  • Developer running 'claude /init' which spawns node to template settings.json (different parent chain — explorer.exe, not npm)
  • Dotfile-management tools (chezmoi, dotbot) syncing .claude config — parent is chezmoi/python, not npm
  • Internal scaffolding generator that writes .claude/settings.json once per repo clone
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "chezmoi.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "dotbot") | where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "claude /init" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName == "Code.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — read the contents of the written .claude/settings.json. Look for 'SessionStart' hook keys and 'node .claude/setup.mjs' commands. Hash .claude/setup.mjs and check for the 498KB obfuscated-bun signature. Step 2: Contain — isolate host. Delete .claude/settings.json and .claude/setup.mjs. Run 'npm install --ignore-scripts' guidance to user. If a Claude Code session ran after the file was written, treat the developer as token-compromised — rotate npm publish tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS/GCP/Azure CLI tokens immediately. Step 3: Hunt — pivot to .vscode/tasks.json writes by same InitiatingProcessId; check ~/.local/share/kitty/cat.py and ~/.config/systemd/user/*.service for sibling persistence. Search GitHub Audit for new repos under user's account with Dune-themed names. Confirm no api.github.com/search/commits polling from python on host.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FolderPath has @"\.claude\" or FolderPath has "/.claude/")
| where FileName in~ ("settings.json","setup.mjs","settings.local.json")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm","node.exe","node","bun.exe","bun","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","bun.exe","npm","node","bun")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          Writer = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          WriterCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\.claude\\settings.json","/.claude/settings.json","\\.claude\\setup.mjs","/.claude/setup.mjs","\\.claude\\settings.local.json")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","node","bun","yarn","pnpm","npx")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VS Code tasks.json folderOpen persistence written by npm install chain AIInstallation Medium
Detects npm/node/bun writing .vscode/tasks.json, the IDE-folderOpen persistence used by the Mini Shai-Hulud AntV wave so the payload re-executes whenever a developer opens the project workspace in VS Code. Legitimate tasks.json is authored by the IDE itself or committed by humans, not by npm install. Rationale: Anchored on article's '.vscode/tasks.json with runOn:folderOpen' persistence claim. Legitimate tasks.json writes come from Code.exe / human edit; npm-as-writer is the discriminator. Hunting tier because some legitimate npm scaffolders (e.g. create-react-app variants) do write workspace tasks — but in combination with the .claude UC firing on same InitiatingProcessId, confidence escalates. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • create-react-app / create-next-app / Vite scaffolders writing tasks.json on project init
  • npm-installed dev tool extension that legitimately templates workspace tasks (e.g. nx CLI workspace generators)
  • Yeoman generator (yo) running under node and producing tasks.json
  • Internal monorepo bootstrap script invoked by npm postinstall
  • VSCode dev container CLI writing workspace configs via node
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("create-react-app","create-next-app","vite create","nx generate","yo ")) | where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName == "Code.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — read the tasks.json content. Hunt for 'runOn': 'folderOpen' combined with shell-command tasks pointing to node /.claude/setup.mjs, bun run index.js, or python ~/.local/share/kitty/cat.py. Confirm the package that triggered the write by walking InitiatingProcessParentId chain to the npm install invocation. Step 2: Contain — delete the malicious tasks.json or revert to the committed version (git checkout). If the developer has opened the workspace in VS Code since the write, treat the host as actively executing the payload and isolate. Step 3: Hunt — correlate to the .claude/settings.json UC and kitty/cat.py UC on same DeviceId. Audit recent npm install history (~/.npm/_logs/) for the compromised AntV package versions.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FolderPath has @"\.vscode\" or FolderPath has "/.vscode/")
| where FileName =~ "tasks.json"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm","node.exe","node","bun.exe","bun","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","bun.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          Writer = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          WriterCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\.vscode\\tasks.json","/.vscode/tasks.json")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","node","bun","yarn","pnpm","npx")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mini Shai-Hulud Linux daemon persistence: kitty/cat.py and systemd user service AIInstallation High
Detects creation of ~/.local/share/kitty/cat.py or ~/.config/systemd/user/*.service by an npm/node/bun process — the OS-level Linux persistence chain that polls GitHub commit search hourly for 'firedalazer'-keyword commands signed with the attacker's 4096-bit RSA-PSS public key. The cat.py + systemd unit combination is article-specific and has near-zero legitimate baseline. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim '~/.local/share/kitty/cat.py' and 'systemd user service' persistence path. The path is misleading by design (looks like the kitty terminal cache) but kitty itself never writes cat.py. Combined with an npm-family writer, the FP rate is effectively zero. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • kitty terminal config writes (kitty.conf, sessions/, themes/) — different filenames, kitty.py would never write a cat.py
  • systemd user service installs by user-level package managers (pipx, cargo install --user, snap) — different writer process
  • Developer manually installing a personal cron-replacement systemd unit (writer is text editor or systemctl, not node)
  • Linux dotfile-management bootstrap (chezmoi apply) writing systemd user units
  • Internal Linux configuration management agent (Ansible-pull as user) — parent is ansible-playbook
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pipx install","cargo install","snap install","systemctl --user enable")) | where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("systemctl","systemd-run"))
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — read cat.py and the .service unit. Look for ExecStart pointing at 'python3 ~/.local/share/kitty/cat.py' and the script body should reference api.github.com/search/commits and 'firedalazer' keyword. Capture SHA256 of cat.py. Step 2: Contain — 'systemctl --user stop' and 'disable' the service unit. Delete cat.py and the .service file. Kill any running python process whose cmdline references cat.py. Treat all credentials accessible to this user account (cloud CLIs, kubeconfig, ~/.npmrc, ~/.ssh/id_*) as compromised — rotate immediately. Step 3: Hunt — search for outbound to t.m-kosche.com from this host (primary C2), api.github.com /search/commits polling, and process events showing python3 reading ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.gcp/credentials, ~/.kube/config. Pivot to GitHub Audit for repo.create events under the user's account.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FolderPath has "/.local/share/kitty/" and FileName =~ "cat.py")
    or (FolderPath has "/.config/systemd/user/" and FileName endswith ".service")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm","node","bun","yarn","pnpm","npx","sh","bash","dash","zsh")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm","node","bun")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          Writer = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentWriter = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          WriterCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (TargetFilePath has "/.local/share/kitty/cat.py")
    or (TargetFilePath has "/.config/systemd/user/" and TargetFilePath endswith ".service")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","node","bun","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash","dash","zsh")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mini Shai-Hulud C2 backchannel: python polling GitHub commit search for 'firedalazer' AICommand & Control High
Detects Python processes reaching api.github.com/search/commits with the 'firedalazer' keyword — the C2 backchannel used by the kitty/cat.py daemon to fetch RSA-PSS-signed command payloads. Hourly poll cadence and the specific search keyword make this article-grade high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim 'polls the GitHub commit search API hourly for commands containing the keyword firedalazer'. The hourly poll cadence (PollCount >= 4 over 7d window catches the daemon while avoiding a one-off curl), python initiator with cat.py in the cmdline, and the unique 'firedalazer' keyword all combine to article-grade fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal devops automation polling api.github.com via python-requests (rare and easy to allowlist by SourceIP)
  • Security researcher manually querying GitHub search API for firedalazer/Shai-Hulud IOC enumeration (low-volume, single host)
  • CI runner with a custom python script syncing release notes from GitHub
  • Snyk/Socket/StepSecurity research scanners polling for IOC propagation
  • GitHub backup-tool sync jobs running under python that happen to hit /search/commits
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("snyk","socket-cli","stepsecurity","pip install")) | where not (DeviceName has_any ("-research","-redteam","-soc-"))
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — get the Python process tree. Confirm parent is kitty/cat.py or systemd-user. Capture cat.py SHA256 and content. Step 2: Contain — isolate the host. Kill the python process and disable the systemd user unit ('systemctl --user disable --now <unit>'). Block api.github.com at egress only for the affected host (don't blanket-block — GitHub is critical). Treat all secrets accessible to that user account as compromised; rotate them. Step 3: Hunt — pivot to GitHub Audit Log for the user's PAT showing /search/commits queries with 'firedalazer'. Search for repos created under user's account with Dune-themed names (UC6). Check for sibling persistence (.claude UC, .vscode UC).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.github.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python.exe","python3","python3.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("cat.py",".local/share/kitty","kitty\\cat.py","firedalazer")
| summarize PollCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP
| where PollCount >= 4
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName =~ "api.github.com" or RequestURL has "api.github.com"
| where RequestURL has "/search/commits" or RequestURL has "firedalazer"
| where RequestClientApplication startswith "python-requests"
| summarize PollCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleUrls = make_set(RequestURL, 5)
          by SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestClientApplication
| where PollCount >= 4
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\python.exe OR *\\python3.exe OR *\\Python.exe OR */python OR */python3) @DestinationHostname:api.github.com @CommandLine:(*cat.py* OR *kitty* OR *firedalazer*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/^api\.github\.com$/i ContextImageFileName=/python(3)?(\.exe)?$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(cat\.py|kitty[\\\/]cat\.py|\.local[\\\/]share[\\\/]kitty|firedalazer)/i}, field=ContextProcessId, key=TargetProcessId, include=[CommandLine])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
| _count >= 4
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.dest="api.github.com" AND (Web.url="*search/commits*" OR Web.url="*firedalazer*") AND (Web.http_user_agent="python-requests*") by host, src, src_user, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | stats count min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime dc(url) as distinct_urls values(http_user_agent) as ua by host, src, src_user | where count >= 4

Mini Shai-Hulud GitHub dead-drop exfiltration via python-requests/2.31.0 AIActions on Objectives High
Detects POST/PUT to api.github.com from a python-requests/2.31.0 User-Agent creating Dune-themed repositories or committing 'results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json' files. This is the article's secondary exfil channel activated when the malware harvests a developer's GitHub PAT, used to stash AES-256-GCM-encrypted credential dumps. Rationale: Anchored on the article's three concrete IOCs: User-Agent string 'python-requests/2.31.0', the exfil filename pattern 'results/results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json', and the Dune-themed repo naming convention (sardaukar/fremen/atreides + sandworm/ornithopter/stillsuit). Triple-anchor (UA + method + path keyword) keeps FP rate well below a generic python-requests-to-github hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1567 T1102.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal Python tooling that legitimately creates GitHub repos via PyGithub or python-requests (rare; usually uses official PyGithub UA)
  • CI/CD pipelines using python-requests to push release artifacts to GitHub releases
  • Security tools (Snyk, Socket, dependency-track) authenticating to api.github.com with python-requests
  • Internal automation pinned to python-requests/2.31.0 — coincidental UA collision (rotate to specific UA strings if hits are noisy)
  • Dune-themed-naming-convention coincidence in a legitimate internal repo (extremely unlikely combined with UA + POST + python-requests)
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("PyGithub","snyk","socket-cli")) | where not (SourceIP in ("<ci-runner-cidr>"))
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — identify the GitHub account whose PAT was used (PAT prefix in proxy auth header if logged, otherwise correlate by SourceIP + SourceUserName). Pull GitHub Audit for repo.create events from that user in the last 7d; flag any matching the Dune keyword regex. Step 2: Contain — revoke the user's GitHub PAT and OAuth tokens via GitHub Enterprise admin. Delete the dead-drop repos. Treat ALL data the developer had on disk as exfiltrated (AWS/GCP/Azure tokens, npm tokens, SSH keys, k8s configs, ~/.netrc). Rotate every credential listed in Stage 4 of the article. Step 3: Hunt — pivot to UC1 (npm→bun) and UC4 (kitty/cat.py) on the same host. Search for hash a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c across the fleet. Check whether any of the user's npm publish tokens were used in the 24h window (npm Audit log) — token may be in the worm-propagation pipeline.
let SuspiciousPython = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ ("python.exe","python","python3.exe","python3")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cat.py",".local/share/kitty","kitty\\cat.py")
    | project DeviceId, ProcessId, PyStart=Timestamp, PyCmd=ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.github.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python","python3.exe","python3")
| join kind=inner SuspiciousPython on DeviceId, $left.InitiatingProcessId == $right.ProcessId
| summarize Connections = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleUrls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 5), SampleCmd = any(PyCmd)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName =~ "api.github.com"
| where RequestClientApplication startswith "python-requests/2.31"
| where RequestMethod in ("POST","PUT","PATCH")
| where RequestURL has_any ("/user/repos","/contents/results-","sardaukar","fremen","atreides","sandworm","ornithopter","stillsuit","harkonnen")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, SentBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Mini Shai-Hulud GitHub dead-drop exfiltration (Dune-themed repos via python-requests)
id: 8a1b5c3d-4e7f-4b9c-9a2e-1d6f8c4b3e7a
description: Detects POST/PUT to api.github.com from python-requests/2.31.0 creating Dune-themed dead-drop repos or committing results-<ts>.json — the Mini Shai-Hulud AntV credential-dump exfiltration channel.
references:
  - https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/19
tags:

  - attack.t1102.003

logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
  selection_host:
    cs-host: 'api.github.com'
  selection_ua:
    cs-user-agent|startswith: 'python-requests/2.31'
  selection_method:
    cs-method:
      - 'POST'
      - 'PUT'
      - 'PATCH'
  selection_path:
    cs-uri-stem|contains:
      - '/user/repos'
      - '/contents/results-'
      - 'sardaukar'
      - 'fremen'
      - 'atreides'
      - 'sandworm'
      - 'ornithopter'
      - 'stillsuit'
  condition: selection_host and selection_ua and selection_method and selection_path
level: high
@http.url_details.host:api.github.com @http.useragent:python-requests/2.31.0* @http.method:(POST OR PUT OR PATCH) @http.url:(*/user/repos* OR */contents/results-* OR *sardaukar* OR *fremen* OR *atreides* OR *sandworm* OR *ornithopter* OR *stillsuit*)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/python(3)?(\.exe)?$/i RemotePort=443
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/^api\.github\.com$/i}, field=aid, key=aid, include=[DomainName])
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(cat\.py|kitty[\\\/]cat\.py|results-\d+|sardaukar|fremen|atreides|sandworm|ornithopter|stillsuit)/i}, field=ContextProcessId, key=TargetProcessId, include=[CommandLine])

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1204.002

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or SHA1 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or MD5 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or SHA1 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or MD5 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

mistralai 2.4.6 dropper: curl downloading transformers.pyz from 83.142.209.194 AIDelivery Medium
Detects the first-stage download performed by the malicious _run_background_task function in mistralai 2.4.6 — a curl invocation with TLS verification disabled (-k) fetching transformers.pyz from the hard-coded attacker IP 83.142.209.194. The combination of binary, flags, target IP, and output filename is unique to this campaign. Rationale: Combines three high-fidelity strings from the article: the literal C2 IP (83.142.209.194), the dropped filename (transformers.pyz), and the curl binary. Each on its own would be specific; the conjunction is unique to this campaign. The python parent and -k (TLS-verify-off) flag are additional confirming pivots from the dropper code reproduced verbatim in GHSA-wx9m-wx4f-4cmg. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wx9m-wx4f-4cmg • https://github.com/mistralai/client-python/issues/523 • https://pypi.org/project/mistralai/
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.002 T1573.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal CI/CD pipeline that intentionally downloads a python zipapp named transformers.pyz from an internal Hugging Face mirror (extremely unlikely with this exact IP)
  • Security researcher fetching the malicious sample for analysis in a sandbox environment
  • Threat-intel ingestion job pulling the IOC for retro-hunting (verify source IP is not the attacker's)
  • Penetration test or purple-team replay of this advisory's TTPs against the same host
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("researcher-svc", "malware-sandbox-svc") // tune to your malware-research / detection-engineering accounts
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the parent-process tree for the curl invocation — confirm parent is python(N) and grandparent is the application that did `import mistralai`. Capture the running user's home directory, identify which credential material lives in it (cloud SDK creds, SSH keys, .env files, ~/.aws/, ~/.config/gcloud, browser-data). Check `pip show mistralai` and lockfiles for version 2.4.6. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host. Kill any process running /tmp/transformers.pyz. Treat the host as compromised — rotate every credential reachable from the importing process per the GHSA recommendation. Block 83.142.209.194 at the egress proxy/firewall. Step 3 (hunt): Search all Linux hosts in the estate for /tmp/transformers.pyz on disk and for any DNS/IP egress to 83.142.209.194 since 2026-05-12 00:05 UTC. Audit CI/CD pipeline images and base layers — anything that ran `pip install mistralai` without version pinning between 2026-05-12 and the PyPI quarantine is suspect.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "curl"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "83.142.209.194"
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "transformers.pyz" and ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/")
| extend TlsVerifyDisabled = ProcessCommandLine has " -k" or ProcessCommandLine has "--insecure"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentFile = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          TlsVerifyDisabled, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DvcOs has_any ("linux", "Linux")
| where TargetProcessName has "curl"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "83.142.209.194"
     or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "transformers.pyz" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/")
| extend TlsVerifyDisabled = TargetProcessCommandLine has " -k" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "--insecure"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TlsVerifyDisabled
| order by TimeGenerated desc

mistralai 2.4.6 dropper: Python interpreter executing /tmp/transformers.pyz as detached session AIInstallation High
Detects the second stage of the mistralai 2.4.6 supply-chain dropper — a python interpreter (sys.executable) executing the dropped /tmp/transformers.pyz zipapp. The python-runs-pyz-from-tmp pattern is the actual code-execution moment; combined with /tmp/ the false-positive rate is near zero. Rationale: Built directly on the Popen invocation in the GHSA's reproduced source: Popen([sys.executable, '/tmp/transformers.pyz'], start_new_session=True). Python interpreter running a .pyz from /tmp is itself unusual; the exact filename transformers.pyz makes this a campaign IOC. The python-parent-spawning-python relationship is the byproduct of subprocess.Popen with sys.executable. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wx9m-wx4f-4cmg • https://github.com/mistralai/client-python/issues/523
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1195.002 T1106
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually testing a python zipapp packaged as transformers.pyz in /tmp (extremely unusual filename collision)
  • Custom internal tool that ships a python zipapp into /tmp during install — verify name and provenance
  • DFIR sandbox replaying this exact campaign for training (whitelist the sandbox host)
  • CI runner that downloads HuggingFace transformers as a zipapp (uncommon distribution mode for that library)
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("malware-research", "dfir-sandbox") // accounts authorised to detonate the sample
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): On the firing host, capture /tmp/transformers.pyz (hash + retain), the parent python's command-line and CWD, and the importing application identity (compare InitiatingProcessParentFileName and the python -c / -m flag). Confirm pip show mistralai reports 2.4.6. Step 2 (contain): Kill the detached zipapp process and any child it spawned. Isolate the host from the network. Delete /tmp/transformers.pyz only after capture. Rotate ALL credentials reachable from the python process (env vars, ~/.aws, ~/.config, ~/.netrc, ~/.ssh, kubeconfig, instance metadata role credentials). Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all Linux hosts for /tmp/transformers.pyz, for processes whose command-line contains '/tmp/' and '.pyz', and for the mistralai 2.4.6 package in any Python venv since 2026-05-12. Pivot to network egress to 83.142.209.194 to find hosts where the download stage succeeded.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName matches regex @"^python[0-9.]*$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/transformers.pyz"
     or (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/tmp/[^\s]+\.pyz(\s|$)")
| extend ParentIsPython = InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"^python[0-9.]*$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          ParentIsPython
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DvcOs has_any ("linux", "Linux")
| where TargetProcessName matches regex @"python[0-9.]*$"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/transformers.pyz"
     or (TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/tmp/[^\s]+\.pyz(\s|$)")
| extend ParentIsPython = ActingProcessName matches regex @"python[0-9.]*$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentIsPython
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound network connection to mistralai 2.4.6 dropper C2 (83.142.209.194) AICommand & Control High
Detects any host in the estate establishing an outbound connection to the attacker-controlled IP 83.142.209.194 referenced in GHSA-wx9m-wx4f-4cmg as the host serving the second-stage transformers.pyz payload. Any connection to this IP is high-confidence evidence the dropper-download stage ran. Rationale: Pure IOC-match on the C2 IP referenced verbatim in the GHSA-wx9m-wx4f-4cmg advisory and reproduced from public issue #523. Hardcoded into the dropper at https://83.142.209.194/transformers.pyz — any tenant connection to this IP is by definition this campaign. Pivot to InitiatingProcessFileName/Command to identify whether curl, python, or another binary did the call (telemetry vendor varies). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wx9m-wx4f-4cmg • https://github.com/mistralai/client-python/issues/523
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feeds or IOC-validation scanners pinging the IP from a dedicated sensor host
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys) included in retro-hunt enrichment that touch the IOC for fingerprinting
  • DFIR responder reachability-testing the host (curl/nc/dig from a jump box)
  • Pre-existing legitimate use of the IP by a third-party SaaS that happens to share the address (very unlikely; verify ASN before discounting)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in ("ti-sensor-01", "sandbox-detonate-02") // tune to your IOC-validation hosts
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the originating host and process from InitiatingProcessFileName / InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm curl/python lineage. Pull /tmp/transformers.pyz from the host if present; hash and retain. Confirm whether mistralai 2.4.6 is installed in any venv on that host (find / -path '*mistralai*' -name 'METADATA' -o -name 'PKG-INFO'). Step 2 (contain): Block 83.142.209.194 at the egress proxy, NGFW, and cloud-egress NACL/Security Group. Isolate the originating host. Force credential rotation per the GHSA recommendation. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep firewall and EDR network telemetry for any connection to 83.142.209.194 since 2026-05-12 00:05 UTC across the full estate (this is the campaign-start timestamp from issue #523). Pull DNS resolutions for that IP. Audit pip-installs, lockfiles, container images, and Docker layer caches built between 2026-05-12 and the PyPI quarantine for the mistralai==2.4.6 string.

Drop of /tmp/transformers.pyz on Linux endpoint AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the dropper artifact /tmp/transformers.pyz on disk — the specific filename and path written by the malicious mistralai 2.4.6 _run_background_task function. Even if the second-stage execution fails or is killed, the file write is a definitive forensic indicator the dropper ran. Rationale: Hard-IOC match on the exact filename + path written by the dropper code reproduced in the GHSA: curl ... -o /tmp/transformers.pyz. This persists on disk even if MISTRAL_INIT is set (which prevents re-download but doesn't delete the file). The advisory explicitly recommends `ls -la /tmp/transformers.pyz` as the affected-host check — this UC is the telemetry-side equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wx9m-wx4f-4cmg • https://github.com/mistralai/client-python/issues/523
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DFIR analyst manually placing the captured malicious sample at this path during analysis on a sandbox
  • Research host re-downloading the IOC for verification (whitelist the analyst's UID/host)
  • Backup/restore tooling restoring a previously-quarantined sample to /tmp
  • Coincidental naming collision — an unrelated python zipapp legitimately named transformers.pyz (extremely unlikely given HF's transformers library is not distributed as a zipapp)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("malware-research", "dfir-evidence-svc") // explicit research accounts
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture the file (cp /tmp/transformers.pyz to evidence store), record its SHA256 and size, confirm the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName should be curl). Check `printenv | grep MISTRAL_INIT` on the host and the importing process's env. Run `pip show mistralai` in every active Python venv on the host. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host. Kill any running python process that has /tmp/transformers.pyz mapped or executing. Delete the file only after capture. Rotate every credential reachable from the importing process — env vars, ~/.aws/, ~/.config/, ~/.netrc, ~/.ssh/, kubeconfig, IMDS role tokens. Step 3 (hunt): Estate-wide sweep for /tmp/transformers.pyz on every Linux host. Cross-reference with the connection-to-83.142.209.194 detection to find hosts where the download succeeded but the file was already cleaned up. Pull all CI/CD job logs and container build histories since 2026-05-12 00:05 UTC that ran pip install of unpinned mistralai.

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6dbaa43bf2f3c0d3cddbca74967e952da563fb974c1ef9d4ecbb2e58e41fe81b") or SHA1 in~ ("6dbaa43bf2f3c0d3cddbca74967e952da563fb974c1ef9d4ecbb2e58e41fe81b") or MD5 in~ ("6dbaa43bf2f3c0d3cddbca74967e952da563fb974c1ef9d4ecbb2e58e41fe81b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6dbaa43bf2f3c0d3cddbca74967e952da563fb974c1ef9d4ecbb2e58e41fe81b") or SHA1 in~ ("6dbaa43bf2f3c0d3cddbca74967e952da563fb974c1ef9d4ecbb2e58e41fe81b") or MD5 in~ ("6dbaa43bf2f3c0d3cddbca74967e952da563fb974c1ef9d4ecbb2e58e41fe81b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6dbaa43bf2f3c0d3cddbca74967e952da563fb974c1ef9d4ecbb2e58e41fe81b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
